collection_title: Chapter 7: Characters, Strings, and the StringBuilder
collection_intro: Short, ungraded practice checks, one for each section of Chapter 7 of *Java Programming*, 10th edition. Rate your confidence, answer, and read the feedback: the review at the end points you to exactly what to re-read.

checks.title: Understanding String Data Problems
checks.subtitle: Why == misjudges two equal names, and the three classes Java offers for text
checks.intro: A program asks Carmen for her name, she types `Carmen`, and it tells her that is not her name. Four questions on why, and on the classes Java gives you for working with text.
takeaways: A `String` variable is a reference: it holds the memory address of a `String` object, not the characters themselves.
`==` on two `String`s asks whether both refer to the same object in memory. Text typed at run time lands in a new object, so `==` can report a difference even when every character matches.
Java splits text work across three kinds of class: `Character` for one character, `String` for text that never changes, and `StringBuilder`/`StringBuffer` for text you will keep modifying.

questions.stem: The user types `Carmen` and presses Enter. What does this code print?

code.label: Java

options.feedback: `nextLine()` builds a new `String` object from what was typed, stored at its own address. `==` compares the two addresses, and they differ even though the characters match.
This reads `==` as comparing letters. For `String`s, `==` compares the memory addresses the two variables hold, and the typed name lives somewhere other than the literal `"Carmen"`.

options.text: Nothing: it does not compile, because `==` cannot compare `String`s
options.feedback: `==` compiles with any two references; it is `<` and `>` that refuse `String` operands. The real trouble is quieter: the code runs and gives a misleading answer.

questions.hint: When Java evaluates `aName == anotherName`, what exactly is stored in each of those two variables?
questions.explanation: `String` is a class, so a `String` variable holds a memory address. `==` compares those addresses, which tells you whether two variables refer to the same object, not whether two objects contain the same characters.
questions.aside: Java keeps a single shared copy of each identical string literal in a program, so two literals can pass an `==` test. That makes this bug sneaky: a quick test with literals seems to work, and the failure appears only with real input.

questions.concept: A String variable is a reference
questions.stem: After `String aGreeting = "Hello";` runs, what is stored in the memory location named `aGreeting`?

options.text: The address of the memory where the characters `Hello` are stored
options.feedback: A `String` variable is a reference. It records where the `Hello` object lives, not the letters themselves; that is why comparing two such variables compares locations.

options.text: The characters `Hello` themselves, just as `int x = 10;` stores 10
options.feedback: That is how primitive variables work. The shortcut declaration makes `String` look primitive, but `String` is a class and its variables hold addresses.

options.text: The number 5, the count of characters in the text it names
options.feedback: You can ask a `String` for its length, but the variable itself does not store it; it stores where the object is.

options.text: A copy of the whole `String` class, ready to hold any text
options.feedback: A variable never holds a class. It holds a reference to one object created from that class.

questions.hint: Is `String` a primitive type like `int`, or a class? What does a variable of a class type hold?
questions.explanation: Variables of primitive types hold their values directly. Variables of class types, including `String`, hold a reference: the memory address of an object. Most surprises with `String` comparisons come from forgetting this.

questions.stem: Looking at the Carmen program, a classmate concludes: "Java says the names differ, so the user must have typed an extra space." What is the flaw in that reasoning?

options.text: `==` compared memory addresses, so matching text can still come out as different
options.feedback: The comparison never looked at the letters. Two objects with identical characters at different addresses are different to `==`, with or without a stray space.

options.text: There is no flaw: a hidden trailing space is the only way two equal names can differ
options.feedback: A trailing space would make the *contents* differ, but `==` never inspects contents. A perfectly typed name gives the same result.

options.text: `nextLine()` keeps the newline from the Enter key, and that newline is what differs
options.feedback: `nextLine()` returns the line without its line ending. The real cause is that `==` compares where the objects are stored.

options.text: `==` compares only the first character of each name, so the error is in the case of `C`
options.feedback: `==` does not compare characters at all when its operands are objects; it compares the two references as a whole.

questions.hint: Would the result change if the user typed the name perfectly? What is `==` actually comparing?
questions.explanation: When a result looks wrong, check what the operation really measures before blaming the data. For objects, `==` measures identity (same address), so equal-looking text in two separate objects always compares as different.

questions.stem:
Match each task to the class the reading recommends.

(1) Test whether a single typed key is a digit.
(2) Store a customer ID that never changes.
(3) Build a report by adding text to it thousands of times.

options.feedback: Each class fits one kind of data: a single character, fixed text, and text that keeps changing. Choosing by that question is the habit to keep.
`String` can hold all three, but it is meant for unchanging text, and single-character tests belong to `Character`. Changing a `String` thousands of times creates thousands of new objects.
This swaps fixed and changeable data. `String` is for text that never changes; `StringBuilder` is the one built for repeated modification.
`Character` holds exactly one character, so it cannot store a whole ID, and `StringBuilder` is for changeable text rather than single-character tests.

questions.hint: For each task ask two things: is it one character or many, and will the text change after it is created?
questions.explanation: `Character` holds and inspects one character. `String` holds fixed text made of one or more characters. `StringBuilder` and `StringBuffer` hold text that you plan to change.
questions.ref: Ch. 7.1, the list of text classes (p. 238)

checks.title: Using Character Class Methods
checks.subtitle: Comparing char values, is- versus to- methods, and testing letters, digits and whitespace
checks.intro: A sign-up form has to check each character of a password: is it a digit, a letter, a symbol? Five questions on the tools that inspect one character at a time.
takeaways: `char` is primitive, so `==`, `<` and `>` compare characters directly by their Unicode values, and every uppercase letter comes before every lowercase one.
`Character` methods named `is…` answer a question with a `boolean`; methods named `to…` return a converted `char` and leave anything that isn't a letter unchanged.
These methods are `static`: call them on the class, as in `Character.isDigit(c)`, and pass the character in as the argument.

questions.stem: What does this code print?

options.feedback: `'7'` is a digit, so it also passes the letter-or-digit test. Digits have no case: `isUpperCase()` is false and `toUpperCase()` hands the character back unchanged.
`isLetterOrDigit()` is true when *either* condition holds, and being a digit is enough.
This treats "not lowercase" as "uppercase". A digit is neither, so `isUpperCase()` returns false.

options.text: `true true false`, then an error at `toUpperCase(c)`
options.feedback: `toUpperCase()` makes no change when its argument isn't a lowercase letter. It simply returns `'7'`.

questions.hint: Does a digit have an uppercase or lowercase form? What does Table 7-1 say `toUpperCase()` does when there is nothing to convert?
questions.explanation: `isLetterOrDigit()` is true for anything that is a letter or a digit. Case belongs only to letters, so for a digit both `isUpperCase()` and `isLowerCase()` are false, and the `to…` methods return it unchanged.

questions.concept: is… returns boolean, to… returns char
questions.stem: A student wants to print a message when `ch` is uppercase. What happens with this code?

options.text: It does not compile: an `if` condition must be a `boolean`, not a `char`
options.feedback: The `to` prefix means "convert and return a character". A condition needs a `boolean`, which is what the `is` methods return; `isUpperCase(ch)` was the intended call.

options.text: It prints `Uppercase!`, because `ch` is converted to `Q` before the test
options.feedback: Converting `ch` doesn't produce a condition. `toUpperCase()` returns `'Q'`, and Java won't treat a character as true or false.

options.text: It prints nothing, because `q` is a lowercase letter, not an uppercase one
options.feedback: That is what `isUpperCase(ch)` would do. With `toUpperCase(ch)` the program never runs: the compiler rejects a `char` used as a condition.

options.text: It compiles, but stops with an error when the `if` statement is reached
options.feedback: A type mismatch like this is found by the compiler, before the program can run.

questions.hint: Look at the method's prefix. What type does a `to…` method give back, and what type must an `if` condition be?
questions.explanation: The prefix tells you the return type: `is…` methods return `boolean` and can be used as conditions; `to…` methods return a converted `char`. Java never converts a `char` to `true` or `false`, so using one as a condition is a compile-time error.
questions.ref: Ch. 7.2, Table 7-1 and Two Truths & a Lie (pp. 239–240)

questions.stem: What does this code print?

code.label: Java

options.feedback: `char` comparisons use Unicode values. Every uppercase letter has a smaller value than every lowercase letter, so `'Z'` (90) is less than `'b'` (98).
In the alphabet b comes before z, but the comparison uses Unicode values, where all uppercase letters come before all lowercase ones.

options.text: Nothing: it does not compile, because `<` cannot compare characters
options.feedback: That rule is about `String`s. `char` is a primitive type, so relational operators work on it directly.

questions.hint: Characters are compared by their Unicode values. Where do the uppercase letters sit relative to the lowercase ones?
questions.explanation: Because `char` is primitive, `<` and `>` compare characters by Unicode value. Within one case this matches alphabetical order, but uppercase letters (65–90) all come before lowercase letters (97–122).
questions.aside: Each lowercase letter is exactly 32 above its uppercase partner: `'A'` is 65 and `'a'` is 97. In binary, 32 is a single bit, so changing a letter's case flips just one bit. Section 7.3 uses the same gap of 32 to spot case differences.

questions.stem: A password checker counts characters that are **not** letters or digits. (`charAt(i)` returns the character at position `i`.) What does it print?

code.label: Java

options.feedback: Two characters fail `isLetterOrDigit()`: the space and `@`. A space is neither a letter nor a digit, so it is counted; to skip it you would also test `isWhitespace()`.
This counts only `@`, as if spaces were ignored. `isLetterOrDigit()` is false for a space, so the `!` makes it count.
This also counts `1`, but a digit passes `isLetterOrDigit()`, so the `!` makes the condition false for it.
These are the characters that *pass* the test: four letters and a digit. The `!` reverses the test, so they are the ones not counted.

questions.hint: Go through the seven characters one by one. Which of them are neither a letter nor a digit?
questions.explanation: `isLetterOrDigit()` is false for punctuation, symbols *and* whitespace such as a space or tab. When a rule should treat spaces differently from symbols, test `isWhitespace()` separately.
questions.ref: Ch. 7.2, Table 7-1 and Two Truths & a Lie (pp. 239–240)

questions.stem: Why does the reading write `Character.isDigit(c)` rather than `c.isDigit()` for a `char` variable `c`?

options.text: `isDigit()` is `static`, and a primitive `char` has no methods of its own
options.feedback: The class name before the dot marks a `static` method. `c` is a primitive, not an object, so it can't be the target of a call; it goes in as the argument.

options.text: `Character` must be named so that Java can import it from `java.lang`
options.feedback: Everything in `java.lang` is imported into every program automatically. The class name is there because the method belongs to the class.

options.text: Both forms work, and `Character.` is only a convention for readability
options.feedback: `c.isDigit()` does not compile: `c` is a primitive `char`, and primitive values have no methods.

options.text: `isDigit()` is defined in `String`, so it needs a class name in front
options.feedback: `isDigit()` belongs to the `Character` class (Table 7-1). Calling through a class name is what marks a method as `static`.

questions.hint: What does it tell you when a method is called with a class name, a dot, and the method name, with no object in front?
questions.explanation: A method called as `ClassName.method()` is `static`: it belongs to the class and works on the arguments you pass. `char` values are primitives, so the `Character` class supplies static methods that take a `char` and inspect or convert it.
questions.aside: Unicode has many letters and digits beyond A–Z and 0–9. `Character.isDigit('٣')` (Arabic-Indic three) and `Character.isLetter('é')` both return `true`, so these methods work on names and numbers typed in many languages.

checks.title: Declaring and Comparing String Objects
checks.subtitle: References and immutability, equals() versus ==, compareTo(), and empty versus null
checks.intro: A sign-up page lets `Carmen` and `carmen` register as different people, and the sorted member list puts `Zoe` before `adam`. Six questions on comparing text the way you meant to.
takeaways: Strings are immutable: assigning a new value points the variable at a new object, and the old characters never change.
Compare contents with `equals()`, or `equalsIgnoreCase()` when case shouldn't matter; `==` only tells you whether two references point at the same object.
`compareTo()` returns 0, a negative or a positive number taken from the first pair of differing characters' Unicode values, so uppercase sorts before lowercase.

questions.concept: == and equals() with literals and new
questions.stem: What does this code print?

code.label: Java

options.feedback: Identical literals are stored once, so `a` and `b` hold the same address. `new` creates a separate object, so `a == c` is false. `equals()` compares the characters, which match.
This treats `==` as a content test. `new String("abc")` builds a second object at its own address, so `==` sees two different references.
Two identical literals share one stored copy, so `a == b` is true. That sharing is what makes `==` seem to work in quick tests.
`equals()` ignores where the objects are stored and compares their characters, which are identical.

questions.hint: Which of these lines creates a brand-new object, and which reuse a value already stored in memory?
questions.explanation: Initializing two `String`s to the same literal stores the value once, so both references hold the same address. `new` always creates another object. Only `equals()` reliably answers "same characters?", however the `String`s were created.
questions.aside: Calling `intern()` on a `String` returns the shared stored copy: `new String("abc").intern() == "abc"` is `true`. Java stores literals this way so a program doesn't keep many copies of the same text.

questions.stem: What does this code print?

options.feedback: The first three letters match. At the fourth, `g` meets `e`; `g` is two letters after `e`, so the result is 2, a positive number meaning `Morgan` sorts after `Moreno`.
This subtracts the wrong way round. The result is the calling string's character minus the argument's: `g` − `e` = 2.
`compareTo()` doesn't only return 1 or −1; it returns the size of the first difference in Unicode values.
Both names have six letters, but `compareTo()` compares characters, not lengths, and they differ at the fourth letter.

questions.hint: Walk through the two names one character at a time until they differ. How far apart are those two characters?
questions.explanation: `compareTo()` scans both `String`s from the start and stops at the first differing pair of characters. It returns the calling string's character value minus the argument's: zero for identical text, negative for "less than", positive for "more than".
questions.ref: Ch. 7.3, compareTo() and the Roger/Rodrigo example (pp. 244–245)

questions.stem: What does this code print?

code.label: Java

options.feedback: `'a'` (97) minus `'B'` (66) is positive, so `apple` counts as "more" and the `else` branch runs. In Unicode every uppercase letter comes before every lowercase one.
That is dictionary order, which ignores case. `compareTo()` uses Unicode values, and uppercase `B` has a smaller value than lowercase `a`.

options.text: Nothing: it does not compile, because `<` cannot be used with `String`s
options.feedback: Here `<` compares the `int` that `compareTo()` returns, not the `String`s themselves, so it compiles.

questions.hint: Only the first characters matter here. Which has the smaller Unicode value: lowercase `a` or uppercase `B`?
questions.explanation: `compareTo()` is a lexicographical comparison based on Unicode values, not true alphabetical order. Because all uppercase letters come before all lowercase letters, mixed-case words sort in surprising ways unless you put them in the same case first.
questions.aside: `String` also offers `compareToIgnoreCase()`, which compares as if both strings had the same case, so `"apple"` comes before `"Banana"` the way a dictionary would order them.
questions.ref: Ch. 7.3, compareTo() and the Note on Unicode case values (pp. 244–245)

questions.stem: A program asks *Continue? (yes/no)* and stores the reply in the `String` named `answer`. Users type `yes`, `Yes` or `YES`. Which condition accepts all three?

options.feedback: It compares the characters while treating upper- and lowercase as the same, which is exactly the uncertainty Shift and Caps Lock create.
`equals()` is case sensitive: `"Yes"` and `"yes"` differ in their first character, so only one of the three replies passes.
Lowering the case is a good idea, but `toLowerCase()` returns a new object at its own address, and `==` compares addresses, so this is false even for `yes`.
Zero means an exact match, case included, so `Yes` and `YES` give nonzero results.

questions.hint: You need a content comparison that treats `Y` and `y` as the same letter.
questions.explanation: `equals()` returns true only for identical contents, case included. `equalsIgnoreCase()` compares contents but ignores case, which suits input typed by people.

questions.stem: What happens when this code runs?

code.label: Java

options.text: It prints `false`, then stops with an error on the last line
options.feedback: `word1` refers to a real `String` that happens to be empty, so its methods work. `word2` holds no address at all, so there is no object to call `equals()` on.
That treats `null` like an empty `String`. A null reference refers to no object, so `word2.equals(...)` has nothing to run on.

options.text: It stops with an error on the first comparison, since `word1` holds nothing
options.feedback: An empty `String` is still an object at a real address; it just contains zero characters, and `equals()` works on it.

options.text: It does not compile, because `word2` is set to `null`
options.feedback: Assigning `null` is legal, and the compiler doesn't track which references are null. The problem appears only when the line runs.

questions.hint: One of these variables refers to an object with no characters in it; the other refers to no object at all. Which can a method be called on?
questions.explanation: An empty `String` (`""`) is an object with length zero and supports every `String` method. A null `String` holds no memory address, so calling any method through it causes an error at run time.
questions.aside: Putting the literal first avoids the crash: `"hi".equals(word2)` simply returns `false` when `word2` is null, because a literal is never null. Many Java style guides recommend this order.

questions.stem: What does this code print?

code.label: Java

options.feedback: `saved` received a copy of the address of `Hello`. Assigning `"Bonjour"` gives `greeting` a new address; the `Hello` object is untouched and `saved` still refers to it.
This assumes the assignment rewrote the characters at the shared address. Strings are immutable: the assignment creates a new object and changes only `greeting`.
This assumes `Hello` was discarded once `greeting` moved on. The garbage collector only reclaims objects nothing refers to, and `saved` still refers to `Hello`.

questions.hint: Does `greeting = "Bonjour";` change the characters of an existing object, or change which object `greeting` refers to?
questions.explanation: Strings are never changed in place. Assigning a new value creates a new `String` object and stores its address in the variable; any other variable that held the old address still sees the old text.

checks.title: Using a Variety of String Methods
checks.subtitle: Positions from zero, substring(), case-sensitive searches, and converting between Strings and numbers
checks.intro: A mail-merge greets a customer as "Dear ovelace", and a price calculator adds 12 and 30 to get 1230. Six questions on the `String` methods behind bugs like these.
takeaways: Positions start at 0. `substring(start, end)` includes `start` and stops *before* `end`, so its length is `end − start`; the last valid index is `length() − 1`.
`String` methods never change the `String` they are called on; they return a new one, so keep the result: `s = s.replace(' ', '-');`.
`+` with a `String` joins text. To do arithmetic on text input, convert it first with `Integer.parseInt()` or `Double.parseDouble()`.

questions.stem: What does this code print?

code.label: Java

options.feedback: `indexOf(' ')` is 3 because counting starts at 0. `substring(0, 3)` stops before position 3, giving `Ada`; `substring(4)` runs to the end, giving `Lovelace`.
This includes the end position, which would capture the space too. The second argument is where the substring stops, not its last character.
This counts positions from 1, so the space seems to be at position 4. The first position of a `String` is 0.

options.text: Nothing: `substring()` needs two arguments, so it does not compile
options.feedback: With one argument, `substring()` extends to the end of the original string.

questions.hint: Number the characters of `"Ada Lovelace"` starting from 0. Where is the space, and is the second argument of `substring()` included?
questions.explanation: String positions start at 0. `substring(start, end)` returns the characters from `start` up to but not including `end`, so its length is `end − start`; with only `start`, it runs to the end.

questions.stem: This loop is meant to count the spaces in `sentence`. What happens when it runs?

code.label: Java

options.text: It stops with an error when `x` reaches 5
options.feedback: `length()` is 5, so the valid positions are 0 to 4. The `<=` lets `x` reach 5, and `charAt(5)` asks for a position past the end, which causes an error.
One space would be counted if the loop stopped in time, but `<=` makes it call `charAt(5)` before the `println()` is reached.

options.text: It prints `2`, counting the end of the string as a space
options.feedback: `charAt()` doesn't return a filler character past the end; an index equal to the length is an error.

options.text: It prints `0`, because the loop never reaches the space
options.feedback: The space is at position 2 and the loop does visit it; the problem is the final pass.

questions.hint: List the positions `x` takes. What is the highest position that actually holds a character in a 5-character `String`?
questions.explanation: `charAt()` accepts positions from 0 to `length() − 1`; a negative argument, or one greater than or equal to the length, causes an error. Loops over a `String` therefore use `x < s.length()`, not `<=`.

questions.stem: What does this code print?

options.feedback: `replace()` builds a new `String` and returns it, but this code throws the result away. `partNum` still refers to the original object. `partNum = partNum.replace(' ', '-');` would keep it.
That is the value `replace()` returns, but nothing stores it. Strings are immutable, so calling a method on one can't change it.
`replace()` replaces every occurrence, not only the first, and here even that result is discarded.

options.text: Nothing: it does not compile until the result of `replace()` is stored
options.feedback: Java lets you ignore a method's return value. The code compiles and runs, which is why this mistake is easy to miss.

questions.hint: Strings are immutable. Where could the changed text go, if not into the original object?
questions.explanation: Methods such as `replace()`, `toUpperCase()` and `substring()` return a new `String` and leave the original unchanged. To use the result, assign it, as in `aWord = aWord.toUpperCase();`.

questions.stem: A course search must report whether a query such as `java` appears anywhere in a title such as `Intro to Java Programming`, however either is capitalized. Which condition does that?

options.feedback: `contains()` is case sensitive, so the fix the reading recommends is to convert both `String`s to the same case before searching.
This lowers only the query. The title still holds `Java` with a capital `J`, and `contains()` is case sensitive, so the search misses.
Putting both in one case is right, but `equals()` compares the *whole* title, and `JAVA` is not equal to `INTRO TO JAVA PROGRAMMING`.
Case is handled, but `startsWith()` checks only the beginning, and this title begins with `intro`, not `java`.

questions.hint: You need a test that finds text anywhere inside the title and ignores case. Which methods are case sensitive?
questions.explanation: `contains()`, `startsWith()`, `endsWith()` and `replace()` are all case sensitive. When case shouldn't matter, convert the participating `String`s to the same case first.
questions.ref: Ch. 7.4, contains() and startsWith() (p. 247); Don't Do It (p. 258)

questions.stem: What does this code print?

code.label: Java

options.feedback: With two `String`s, `+` joins the text. After `parseInt()` converts each one, the operands are `int`s and `+` adds them.
This assumes Java notices the digits and adds them. `+` with `String` operands always concatenates, whatever the characters are.
`parseInt()` returns an `int`, so the second `+` has two numbers to work with and performs arithmetic.
Concatenation joins text exactly as it is and adds no space; you would have to include `" "` yourself.

questions.hint: What are the types of the operands on each side of `+` in the two `println()` calls?
questions.explanation: `+` concatenates when either operand is a `String`, and adds when both are numbers. Text that holds digits must be converted with a wrapper-class method such as `Integer.parseInt()` before you can do arithmetic with it.
questions.ref: Ch. 7.4, concatenation (p. 247) and Converting String Objects to Numbers (pp. 249–250)

questions.stem: An input dialog returns the salary the user typed, `"147.82"`, in the `String` named `entry`. Which statement stores it as a number you can do arithmetic with?

options.feedback: `parseDouble()` is a static method of the `Double` wrapper class that turns the text into a `double` value.
`147.82` is a valid number but the wrong type for `parseInt()`, which reads whole numbers only; it causes a `NumberFormatException`.
A cast can't turn a `String` into a number; the types are unrelated, so this does not compile.
`toString()` goes the other way, turning a number into a `String`.

questions.hint: The text holds a decimal number. Which wrapper class matches that type, and which of its methods reads a `String`?
questions.explanation: Input from `showInputDialog()` or `nextLine()` is always a `String`. Convert it with the parse method of the matching wrapper class: `Integer.parseInt()` for whole numbers, `Double.parseDouble()` for decimals. Text that isn't a valid number of that type causes a `NumberFormatException`.
questions.aside: `Integer.parseInt()` can also read other number bases: `Integer.parseInt("ff", 16)` returns 255, and `Integer.parseInt("101", 2)` returns 5.
questions.ref: Ch. 7.4, Converting String Objects to Numbers (pp. 249–250)

checks.title: Learning About the StringBuilder and StringBuffer Classes
checks.subtitle: Mutable text, capacity and length, append(), insert(), setCharAt(), and when not to use them
checks.intro: A program builds a log one line at a time, and it gets slower with every line it adds. Six questions on the classes made for text that keeps changing.
takeaways: A `StringBuilder` changes in place: `append()`, `insert()`, `setCharAt()` and `setLength()` modify the same object, unlike `String` methods, which return new objects.

Length is the number of characters stored; capacity is the size of the buffer. Built from a `String`, capacity starts at that `String`'s length plus 16, and presizing helps when you know roughly how large it will grow.
`equals()` on two `StringBuilder`s compares references, so convert them with `toString()` before comparing contents. Use `String` unless the text changes often.

questions.stem: What does this code print?

code.label: Java
code.text:
StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder("Miami");
System.out.println(sb.length() + " " + sb.capacity());

options.feedback: The length is the 5 characters stored. Built from a `String`, the capacity is that length plus 16 extra positions: 21.
16 is the extra room, but it is *added* to the length of the initial `String`, not used on its own.
`length()` counts only the characters actually stored, not the empty positions in the buffer.
The buffer is made larger than the text, with 16 spare positions, so it can grow without allocating new memory.

questions.hint: One method counts the characters stored; the other reports the size of the buffer. How much extra room does the constructor add?
questions.explanation: A `StringBuilder` keeps its characters in a buffer that can be larger than the text. `length()` reports the characters stored; `capacity()` reports the buffer size, which starts at the initial `String`'s length plus 16.
questions.aside: When a `StringBuilder` outgrows its buffer, the standard JDK allocates a new one about twice as large (old capacity × 2 + 2) and copies every character across. That copying is the extra time the reading's timing program measures.

questions.stem: What does this code print?

code.label: Java

options.feedback: `insert(0, ...)` puts `Black` at the front and `append()` adds to the end, giving `Blackbirds sing`. Position 5 holds the `b` of `birds`, and `setCharAt()` replaces it.
`setCharAt()` replaces the character at a position; it does not insert a new one the way `insert()` does.
This counts positions from 1, so position 5 lands on `k`. The first character of a `StringBuilder` is at position 0.
This treats `StringBuilder` like `String`, whose methods return new objects. These methods change the object itself, so no reassignment is needed.

questions.hint: Write out the contents after each line, numbering positions from 0. Does `setCharAt()` add a character or swap one?
questions.explanation: `append()` adds to the end, `insert()` adds at a given position, and `setCharAt()` replaces one character. All of them change the same `StringBuilder` object, and positions start at 0, as in a `String`.

options.feedback: On `StringBuilder` objects `equals()` compares references, and these are two separate objects. After `toString()`, `String`'s `equals()` compares the characters, which match.
This assumes `equals()` compares contents for every class. That's true of `String`, but a `StringBuilder`'s `equals()` compares references.
`toString()` produces two `String`s, and `String`'s `equals()` does compare contents, so the second test is true.
This has the two tests reversed: the direct `equals()` is the reference comparison, and the `toString()` version compares the text.

questions.hint: Which class's `equals()` runs in each test, and what does each version compare?
questions.explanation: `equals()` compares contents for `String` objects but references for `StringBuilder` objects. To compare the text in two builders, convert both with `toString()` and compare the resulting `String`s.

options.feedback: A shorter length truncates the string to 4 characters. The buffer is not shrunk, so the capacity stays at 16 + 16 = 32.
Capacity isn't recalculated from the new length; the buffer keeps the size it was given when the object was created.
`setLength()` changes the string itself: a length shorter than the string truncates it.
Length and capacity are separate: `setLength()` changes how many characters are kept, not the size of the buffer.

questions.hint: The initial string has 16 characters. Which of the three values does `setLength(4)` change?
questions.explanation: `setLength()` sets how many characters the `StringBuilder` holds: shorter truncates, longer pads with `'\u0000'` characters. It does not change the capacity, which is the size of the underlying buffer.

questions.stem: A program builds a 50,000-line report by appending one line at a time, and also checks whether each typed command equals `quit`. Which plan follows the reading's advice?

options.text: A presized `StringBuilder` for the report; a `String` for each command
options.feedback: Repeated changes are what `StringBuilder` is for, and presizing avoids reallocating as it grows. Commands are compared, not changed, and comparing contents is `String`'s job.

options.text: `StringBuilder` for both, since it can be used anywhere a `String` is
options.feedback: It can stand in, but the reading warns against it when you need comparisons: a `StringBuilder`'s `equals()` compares references, so `quit` would never match.

options.text: `String` for both, since the garbage collector clears old copies for free
options.feedback: Collection isn't free, and each change to a `String` creates a whole new object and copies its characters, so the cost grows with the report.

options.text: `StringBuffer` for the report, because it is faster than `StringBuilder`
options.feedback: It's the reverse: `StringBuilder` is more efficient. `StringBuffer` adds thread safety, which a single-threaded program doesn't need.

questions.hint: For each piece of text, ask whether it changes repeatedly or is mainly compared.
questions.explanation: Use `StringBuilder` when text changes many times, and give it an approximate capacity if you can estimate the final size. Keep `String` for text that is compared or rarely changed. `StringBuffer` behaves the same but is thread safe, so it is only worth its cost in multithreaded programs.
questions.aside: Before Java 9, the compiler quietly turned `a + b + c` into a chain of `StringBuilder` `append()` calls; newer versions use a faster built-in mechanism. Either way, `s = s + line` inside a loop still creates a new `String` on every pass.

options.feedback: The shortcut that skips `new` exists only for `String`. A `StringBuilder` must be created with `new` and its constructor, as in `new StringBuilder("Hello")`.

options.text: It compiles, and afterward `greeting` holds `Hello there`
options.feedback: That would be the result with `new StringBuilder("Hello")`. Java does not convert a string literal into a `StringBuilder` for you.

options.text: It compiles, but fails at run time because a literal can't be changed
options.feedback: The mismatch between a `String` value and a `StringBuilder` variable is caught by the compiler, before anything runs.

questions.hint: What type is `"Hello"`? Is there a shortcut for creating a `StringBuilder` the way there is for a `String`?
questions.explanation: A string literal is always a `String` object. A `StringBuilder` is created with `new`, the constructor name, and an initial value (or a capacity) in the parentheses; to start from existing text, pass the `String` to the constructor or `append()` it to an empty builder.
